title: I want to play in the style of Marty Friedman
goal: I want to play in the style of Marty Friedman

steps.title: Alternate picking precision
steps.description:
[Before you start]
Advanced roadmap: already keep eight bars of eighth-note rhythm at 90 BPM, play one minor-scale position, identify root/third/fifth, and perform basic hammer-ons, pull-offs and a whole-tone bend. Use a six-string guitar in standard tuning for the written fret examples, a metronome, recorder and pitch reference. Check repertoire tuning against its chosen recording. Keep a short melody alongside the drills from the start: hear it, practise the relevant movement, then apply that movement to the melody. These are refinements to existing steps: your logged sessions and checked resources remain valid, and completed steps do not need to be repeated.

[What it is]
Alternate picking gives successive notes alternating downstrokes and upstrokes.

[Why it matters]
Use it as a coordination baseline, then choose articulation by sound. Strict alternation is not a rule for every Friedman phrase and copying a hand posture is not the goal.

[How to practice]
On B-string frets 5-7-8-7 play sixteenths for one bar, then rest for one bar. Try both starting strokes with a comfortable grip; finish each group cleanly instead of racing.

[Practice check]
The exercise and tempo target are curriculum practice tasks, not transcriptions or claims about the artist's own routine. BPM means quarter notes. Start slower, then use the stated task for self-assessment; listen for missing notes, unintended strings, pitch errors and loss of pulse.

[Sources]
Marty Friedman, Finding Your Path to Musical Individuality: https://www.guitarworld.com/magazine/full-shred-marty-friedman-finding-your-path
steps.successCriteria: Record four play/rest cycles at 70 BPM with each starting stroke, with no missed notes or unintended accents. Use two consecutive clean takes unless another count is specified.

steps.title: String-skipping accuracy
steps.description:
[What it is]
A string skip moves between nonadjacent strings while keeping the intervening string silent.

[Why it matters]
Accurate targeting preserves a wide melodic interval. The linked muting drill supports silence; it does not replace practising the actual skip.

[How to practice]
Alternate G9 and high-e12 as eighth notes, leaving B silent. Add G12 and high-e15 to form a four-note pattern; mute lower strings with the picking hand as needed.

[Practice check]
The exercise and tempo target are curriculum practice tasks, not transcriptions or claims about the artist's own routine. BPM means quarter notes. Start slower, then use the stated task for self-assessment; listen for missing notes, unintended strings, pitch errors and loss of pulse.

[Sources]
Marty Friedman, How to Play Fast Arpeggio-Based Licks Without Sweep Picking: https://www.guitarworld.com/lessons/how-to-play-fast-arpeggio-based-licks-without-sweep-picking
steps.successCriteria: Record eight bars at 70 BPM with no B-string attack, missed target or hesitation at a skip. Use two consecutive clean takes unless another count is specified.

steps.title: Cross-string articulation
steps.description:
[What it is]
Cross-string articulation controls note length and accent when a melody changes strings.

[Why it matters]
This develops the sound of the connection, distinct from simply reaching a skipped string. Friedman demonstrates changing articulation while retaining a melody.

[How to practice]
Play G9-B8-e7-B8 as eighth notes. Record four bars with separated notes, four connected without chord overlap, and four with the first high-E note accented.

[Practice check]
The exercise and tempo target are curriculum practice tasks, not transcriptions or claims about the artist's own routine. BPM means quarter notes. Start slower, then use the stated task for self-assessment; listen for missing notes, unintended strings, pitch errors and loss of pulse.

[Sources]
Marty Friedman, Using Various Articulation Techniques to Expressively Interpret a Melody: https://www.guitarworld.com/magazine/full-shred-marty-friedman-using-various
steps.successCriteria: At 70 BPM, record all three four-bar versions; keep the same notes and rhythm while making each articulation choice audible. Use two consecutive clean takes unless another count is specified.

steps.title: Pick attack shading
steps.description:
[What it is]
Attack shading changes the colour and prominence of a note through pick contact.

[Why it matters]
A repeatable contrast helps a target note stand out without changing the melody. Do not assume digging deeper always makes a brighter sound.

[How to practice]
Play a two-bar A-C-E melody on B-string frets 10-13-17. Compare light and firmer contact, then two picking locations; keep amp settings fixed and change one variable at a time.

[Practice check]
The exercise and tempo target are curriculum practice tasks, not transcriptions or claims about the artist's own routine. BPM means quarter notes. Start slower, then use the stated task for self-assessment; listen for missing notes, unintended strings, pitch errors and loss of pulse.

[Sources]
Marty Friedman, Using Various Articulation Techniques to Expressively Interpret a Melody: https://www.guitarworld.com/magazine/full-shred-marty-friedman-using-various
steps.successCriteria: Record the same melody four times at 60 BPM and identify two reproducible tone differences without changing pitches or note lengths. Use two consecutive clean takes unless another count is specified.

steps.title: Palm mute dynamics
steps.description:
[What it is]
Palm muting changes how long a note rings through contact near the bridge.

[Why it matters]
Control of open and damped notes provides contrast and prevents rhythm parts from obscuring a lead. It is general support technique, not the whole Friedman sound.

[How to practice]
Play low-E eighth notes for four bars: open, lightly damped, tightly damped, then open again. Follow with a held B-string note and a clean stop; avoid pulling the string sharp with pressure.

[Practice check]
The exercise and tempo target are curriculum practice tasks, not transcriptions or claims about the artist's own routine. BPM means quarter notes. Start slower, then use the stated task for self-assessment; listen for missing notes, unintended strings, pitch errors and loss of pulse.

[Sources]
Marty Friedman, Using Various Articulation Techniques to Expressively Interpret a Melody: https://www.guitarworld.com/magazine/full-shred-marty-friedman-using-various
steps.successCriteria: Record two cycles at 80 BPM; all three damping levels remain distinguishable and pitched, and the held lead note is not accidentally choked. Use two consecutive clean takes unless another count is specified.

steps.title: Rhythmic picking displacement
steps.description:
[What it is]
Displacement shifts a complete motif by a subdivision while retaining its internal rhythm.

[Why it matters]
It creates a planned offbeat entry. This differs from loosely playing early or late, which can sound like a timing error.

[How to practice]
Write four eighth notes A-C-E-C. In bar 1 start on beat 1 and rest for two beats; in bar 2 start after an eighth rest and rest for the remaining three eighths. Return to the original entry in bar 3.

[Practice check]
The exercise and tempo target are curriculum practice tasks, not transcriptions or claims about the artist's own routine. BPM means quarter notes. Start slower, then use the stated task for self-assessment; listen for missing notes, unintended strings, pitch errors and loss of pulse.

[Sources]
Marty Friedman, Taking Licks You Have Learned from Others and Making Them Your Own: https://www.guitarworld.com/magazine/full-shred-marty-friedman-taking-licks-youve-learned-others-and
steps.successCriteria: Record four three-bar cycles at 70 BPM; the displaced entry lands on the and of 1 and every return lands on beat 1. Use two consecutive clean takes unless another count is specified.

steps.title: Wide vibrato control
steps.description:
[What it is]
Vibrato varies the pitch of a held note with a chosen width and rate.

[Why it matters]
Friedman uses bends and vibrato to interpret a melody. On a fretted string, do not assume the pitch moves equally above and below the unbent note.

[How to practice]
Hold B-string E at fret 5. Wait two beats, then apply four even bend-and-return pulses over two beats. Compare a narrow and wider version; keep returning to E rather than drifting upward.

[Practice check]
The exercise and tempo target are curriculum practice tasks, not transcriptions or claims about the artist's own routine. BPM means quarter notes. Start slower, then use the stated task for self-assessment; listen for missing notes, unintended strings, pitch errors and loss of pulse.

[Sources]
Marty Friedman, Using String-Bending and Vibrato to Personalize a Melody: https://www.guitarworld.com/lessons/full-shred-marty-friedman-using-string-bending-and-vibrato-personalize-melody
steps.successCriteria: Record four bars of each width at 60 BPM; delayed starts and four pulses are audible, and the note returns to E without choking. Use two consecutive clean takes unless another count is specified.

steps.title: Microtonal bending
steps.description:
[What it is]
Microtonal bending deliberately places a pitch between adjacent semitones.

[Why it matters]
This trains small pitch inflections, but Friedman's documented half-step approaches are not automatically microtones. The linked unison-bend exercise trains matching a target, not quarter-tone vocabulary.

[How to practice]
On B-string fret 5, use a cents tuner to compare unbent E, a 50-cent bend and a 100-cent bend. Hold each for a beat, release, then place the 50-cent inflection as a passing gesture before resolving to E.

[Practice check]
The exercise and tempo target are curriculum practice tasks, not transcriptions or claims about the artist's own routine. BPM means quarter notes. Start slower, then use the stated task for self-assessment; listen for missing notes, unintended strings, pitch errors and loss of pulse.

[Sources]
Marty Friedman, Using String-Bending and Vibrato to Personalize a Melody: https://www.guitarworld.com/lessons/full-shred-marty-friedman-using-string-bending-and-vibrato-personalize-melody
steps.successCriteria: Record five 50-cent targets within 15 cents of the chosen target, plus a two-bar phrase at 60 BPM. Explain the difference between the 50-cent inflection and a semitone approach; this target is an ear-training exercise, not a Friedman tuning system. Use two consecutive clean takes unless another count is specified.

steps.title: Controlled legato runs
steps.description:
[What it is]
Legato sounds a connected group with hammer-ons and pull-offs instead of picking every note.

[Why it matters]
Keep its different attack while preserving the rhythm; it need not sound identical to picked notes. Short groups prepare expressive runs and later arpeggio links.

[How to practice]
On B-string play 5-7-8-7 as sixteenths, picking the first note of each group. Alternate a bar of playing and a bar of rest; end the last group on a sustained E.

[Practice check]
The exercise and tempo target are curriculum practice tasks, not transcriptions or claims about the artist's own routine. BPM means quarter notes. Start slower, then use the stated task for self-assessment; listen for missing notes, unintended strings, pitch errors and loss of pulse.

[Sources]
Marty Friedman, Finding Your Path to Musical Individuality: https://www.guitarworld.com/magazine/full-shred-marty-friedman-finding-your-path
steps.successCriteria: Record four play/rest cycles at 60 BPM, with all four notes audible and evenly spaced, followed by a clean sustained ending. Use two consecutive clean takes unless another count is specified.

steps.title: Pre-bend release accuracy
steps.description:
[What it is]
A pre-bend reaches a target before the string is picked, then releases to a planned pitch.

[Why it matters]
Separating the starting pitch from the release timing makes this a deliberate melodic inflection rather than an accidental fall.

[How to practice]
First play B-string E at fret 5 as a reference. Silently bend D# at fret 4 up a semitone, pick the pre-bent E, then release to D# on beat 3. Follow with fretted E in the next bar; compare the initial pitch with the reference.

[Practice check]
The exercise and tempo target are curriculum practice tasks, not transcriptions or claims about the artist's own routine. BPM means quarter notes. Start slower, then use the stated task for self-assessment; listen for missing notes, unintended strings, pitch errors and loss of pulse.

[Sources]
Marty Friedman, Using String-Bending and Vibrato to Personalize a Melody: https://www.guitarworld.com/lessons/full-shred-marty-friedman-using-string-bending-and-vibrato-personalize-melody
Marty Friedman, How to Develop Melodic Ideas with Interesting Twists: https://www.guitarworld.com/lessons/full-shred-marty-friedman-how-develop-melodic-ideas-interesting-twists
steps.successCriteria: Record five two-bar gestures at 60 BPM. Initial E is within 20 cents before vibrato, each release reaches D# on beat 3 and the following E resolves on beat 1. Use two consecutive clean takes unless another count is specified.

steps.title: Double-stop fingering
steps.description:
[What it is]
Double-stops sound two fretted notes together with controlled intonation.

[Why it matters]
They offer brief harmonic emphasis, but should not be presented as a universal Friedman trademark. The linked two-notes-per-bar task is phrasing support, not simultaneous-note training.

[How to practice]
Play G9 with B8 (E-G), then G10 with B10 (F-A), then return. Use half notes and listen to each voice separately before sounding both together.

[Practice check]
The exercise and tempo target are curriculum practice tasks, not transcriptions or claims about the artist's own routine. BPM means quarter notes. Start slower, then use the stated task for self-assessment; listen for missing notes, unintended strings, pitch errors and loss of pulse.

[Sources]
Marty Friedman, Relocating Familiar Melodic Ideas and Patterns: https://www.guitarworld.com/magazine/full-shred-marty-friedman-relocating-familiar-melodic-ideas-and-patterns-and-down-fretboard
steps.successCriteria: Record eight bars at 60 BPM; both voices sound clearly, move on the written beats and leave other strings silent. Use two consecutive clean takes unless another count is specified.

steps.title: Left-hand muting precision
steps.description:
[What it is]
Fretting-hand muting stops unused strings and releases completed notes.

[Why it matters]
Clear silence lets bends, slides and legato remain distinct under gain. Coordinate with the picking hand for lower strings instead of forcing the fretting hand to mute everything.

[How to practice]
Play a G/B-string four-note phrase as eighth notes followed by two beats of rest. Repeat with a slide and a bend; identify which hand stops each unused string.

[Practice check]
The exercise and tempo target are curriculum practice tasks, not transcriptions or claims about the artist's own routine. BPM means quarter notes. Start slower, then use the stated task for self-assessment; listen for missing notes, unintended strings, pitch errors and loss of pulse.

[Sources]
Marty Friedman, Using Various Articulation Techniques to Expressively Interpret a Melody: https://www.guitarworld.com/magazine/full-shred-marty-friedman-using-various
steps.successCriteria: Record eight bars at 70 BPM clean and then with moderate gain; the intended note sustains, while no extra string rings into the two-beat rest. Use two consecutive clean takes unless another count is specified.

steps.title: Slide and smear control
steps.description:
[What it is]
Slides connect fixed pitches; a smear is a deliberately less-defined approach or departure.

[Why it matters]
Choose where the pitch becomes definite. This keeps expressive movement different from missing a target fret.

[How to practice]
On B-string compare D#4 sliding to E5 with D#4 bending to E. Then slide E5 to A10, arriving on beat 3 after starting on beat 1. Mute the departure only after the target has spoken.

[Practice check]
The exercise and tempo target are curriculum practice tasks, not transcriptions or claims about the artist's own routine. BPM means quarter notes. Start slower, then use the stated task for self-assessment; listen for missing notes, unintended strings, pitch errors and loss of pulse.

[Sources]
Marty Friedman, How to Develop Melodic Ideas with Interesting Twists: https://www.guitarworld.com/lessons/full-shred-marty-friedman-how-develop-melodic-ideas-interesting-twists
Marty Friedman, Using Various Articulation Techniques to Expressively Interpret a Melody: https://www.guitarworld.com/magazine/full-shred-marty-friedman-using-various
steps.successCriteria: Record four bars of each approach at 60 BPM; all target Es and As arrive on the planned beat, with no accidental extra picked note. Use two consecutive clean takes unless another count is specified.

steps.title: Wide interval leaps
steps.description:
[What it is]
A wide leap moves to a distant pitch while preserving the shape of a melody.

[Why it matters]
Hear the destination before finding the fret. This adds melodic intention to the earlier string-targeting drill.

[How to practice]
Over Am sing A-E-A, then play A on G14, E on high-e12 and A on high-e17 as quarter, quarter and half notes. Make a second version in which the last A is down an octave.

[Practice check]
The exercise and tempo target are curriculum practice tasks, not transcriptions or claims about the artist's own routine. BPM means quarter notes. Start slower, then use the stated task for self-assessment; listen for missing notes, unintended strings, pitch errors and loss of pulse.

[Sources]
Marty Friedman, How to Play Fast Arpeggio-Based Licks Without Sweep Picking: https://www.guitarworld.com/lessons/how-to-play-fast-arpeggio-based-licks-without-sweep-picking
steps.successCriteria: Record four bars of each version at 60 BPM; name the fifth and octave relationships and land on each intended pitch without searching. Use two consecutive clean takes unless another count is specified.

steps.title: String-skipping legato
steps.description:
[What it is]
A skipped-string legato phrase combines slurs within a string with a separately articulated landing on another.

[Why it matters]
A pull-off cannot transfer vibration to a nonadjacent string. Plan the new attack rather than requiring an impossible uninterrupted slur across the gap.

[How to practice]
On G-string pick 14, pull to 12, then pick high-e12 and hammer to 15. Play the four events as eighth notes with two beats of rest; keep B muted.

[Practice check]
The exercise and tempo target are curriculum practice tasks, not transcriptions or claims about the artist's own routine. BPM means quarter notes. Start slower, then use the stated task for self-assessment; listen for missing notes, unintended strings, pitch errors and loss of pulse.

[Sources]
Marty Friedman, How to Play Fast Arpeggio-Based Licks Without Sweep Picking: https://www.guitarworld.com/lessons/how-to-play-fast-arpeggio-based-licks-without-sweep-picking
steps.successCriteria: Record eight bars at 60 BPM; the new-string pick is intentional, both slurs speak clearly and the B string stays silent. Use two consecutive clean takes unless another count is specified.

steps.title: Octave displacement phrasing
steps.description:
[What it is]
Octave displacement moves selected notes by an octave without changing their pitch class.

[Why it matters]
It changes the register of a motif while retaining its identity. Note-finding practice helps locate targets but is not the musical result.

[How to practice]
Play A-C-E-C as quarter notes, then move only E up an octave. Write fret choices before playing and compare both versions over an Am drone.

[Practice check]
The exercise and tempo target are curriculum practice tasks, not transcriptions or claims about the artist's own routine. BPM means quarter notes. Start slower, then use the stated task for self-assessment; listen for missing notes, unintended strings, pitch errors and loss of pulse.

[Sources]
Marty Friedman, Relocating Familiar Melodic Ideas and Patterns: https://www.guitarworld.com/magazine/full-shred-marty-friedman-relocating-familiar-melodic-ideas-and-patterns-and-down-fretboard
steps.successCriteria: Record four bars of each version at 60 BPM; only the chosen E changes register and the rhythm stays the same. Use two consecutive clean takes unless another count is specified.

steps.title: Thirds and sixths lines
steps.description:
[What it is]
Thirds and sixths connect two melodic voices at named intervals.

[Why it matters]
Learning the actual intervals prevents a shape from becoming an unexplained pattern. The linked tapping drill is not an interval lesson; no tapping is required for this task.

[How to practice]
Over C, play C-E, D-F, E-G, F-A as broken pairs of eighth notes. Then play E-C above, F-D above, G-E above, A-F above as sixths. Identify major and minor intervals by counting semitones.

[Practice check]
The exercise and tempo target are curriculum practice tasks, not transcriptions or claims about the artist's own routine. BPM means quarter notes. Start slower, then use the stated task for self-assessment; listen for missing notes, unintended strings, pitch errors and loss of pulse.

[Sources]
Marty Friedman, Relocating Familiar Melodic Ideas and Patterns: https://www.guitarworld.com/magazine/full-shred-marty-friedman-relocating-familiar-melodic-ideas-and-patterns-and-down-fretboard
steps.successCriteria: Record four bars of each pattern at 60 BPM; name the notes and distinguish the major/minor thirds and their inverted sixths. Use two consecutive clean takes unless another count is specified.

steps.title: Diagonal string patterns
steps.description:
[What it is]
A diagonal pattern moves through both strings and positions.

[Why it matters]
Plan small shifts to reach a chosen register without treating a long stretch as necessary. Reuse a familiar idea instead of learning disconnected shapes.

[How to practice]
Find E-G-B on D/G strings and again an octave higher on B/high E. Play the lower group, shift during a quarter rest, then play the upper group; write a two-bar rhythm before starting.

[Practice check]
The exercise and tempo target are curriculum practice tasks, not transcriptions or claims about the artist's own routine. BPM means quarter notes. Start slower, then use the stated task for self-assessment; listen for missing notes, unintended strings, pitch errors and loss of pulse.

[Sources]
Marty Friedman, Relocating Familiar Melodic Ideas and Patterns: https://www.guitarworld.com/magazine/full-shred-marty-friedman-relocating-familiar-melodic-ideas-and-patterns-and-down-fretboard
steps.successCriteria: Record four two-bar cycles at 60 BPM; both groups contain the stated notes, with the shift inside its written rest. Use two consecutive clean takes unless another count is specified.

steps.title: Intervallic arpeggio shapes
steps.description:
[What it is]
An intervallic arpeggio changes the order of chord tones rather than always ascending.

[Why it matters]
A reordered chord shape can sound like a melody. Keep the harmonic target audible before adding passing notes.

[How to practice]
Over Am play A-E-C-E as eighth notes, rest two beats, then answer with C-E-A-E. Use comfortable string skips; end the next cycle with a held A.

[Practice check]
The exercise and tempo target are curriculum practice tasks, not transcriptions or claims about the artist's own routine. BPM means quarter notes. Start slower, then use the stated task for self-assessment; listen for missing notes, unintended strings, pitch errors and loss of pulse.

[Sources]
Marty Friedman, How to Play Fast Arpeggio-Based Licks Without Sweep Picking: https://www.guitarworld.com/lessons/how-to-play-fast-arpeggio-based-licks-without-sweep-picking
steps.successCriteria: Record four two-bar cycles at 70 BPM, naming root, fifth and third and retaining the planned rests. Use two consecutive clean takes unless another count is specified.

steps.title: Chromatic enclosures
steps.description:
[What it is]
An enclosure approaches a target from both above and below before landing on it.

[Why it matters]
This gives a defined destination to chromatic motion. Keep it distinct from the later single-neighbour approach exercise.

[How to practice]
Over Am use F-D#-E as three eighth notes beginning on beat 1, hold E through beat 3 and rest beat 4. Repeat with C-A#-B over Em, checking how B fits that chord.

[Practice check]
The exercise and tempo target are curriculum practice tasks, not transcriptions or claims about the artist's own routine. BPM means quarter notes. Start slower, then use the stated task for self-assessment; listen for missing notes, unintended strings, pitch errors and loss of pulse.

[Sources]
Marty Friedman, How to Develop Melodic Ideas with Interesting Twists: https://www.guitarworld.com/lessons/full-shred-marty-friedman-how-develop-melodic-ideas-interesting-twists
steps.successCriteria: Record four bars over each chord at 60 BPM; each target arrives on beat 2 and both surrounding notes remain brief. Use two consecutive clean takes unless another count is specified.

steps.title: Harmonic minor fluency
steps.description:
[What it is]
Harmonic minor raises degree 7 of natural minor.

[Why it matters]
The leading tone connects a dominant chord to a minor tonic; this also prepares the next mode. A scale name alone does not produce Friedman's phrasing.

[How to practice]
Play A-B-C-D-E-F-G#-A in one position as eighth notes. Over E7-Am write two bars that approach A from G# on the chord change, then compare with G natural.

[Practice check]
The exercise and tempo target are curriculum practice tasks, not transcriptions or claims about the artist's own routine. BPM means quarter notes. Start slower, then use the stated task for self-assessment; listen for missing notes, unintended strings, pitch errors and loss of pulse.

[Sources]
Marty Friedman, Exploring the Phrygian-Dominant Mode: https://www.guitarworld.com/magazine/betcha-cant-play-marty-friedman-explores-phrygian-dominant-mode
steps.successCriteria: Record four two-bar phrases at 60 BPM; state all seven notes, identify the raised seventh and resolve G# to A when Am begins. Use two consecutive clean takes unless another count is specified.

steps.title: Phrygian dominant mastery
steps.description:
[What it is]
Phrygian dominant has flat 2 and major 3 and is mode 5 of harmonic minor.

[Why it matters]
Friedman demonstrates C Phrygian dominant, but also leaves that collection within the same lesson. Treat it as one colour rather than a rule for an entire solo.

[How to practice]
Over C5 use C-Db-E-F-G-Ab-Bb-C as eighth notes. Make a two-bar phrase highlighting Db-C and F-E, then repeat with one changed rhythm. Compare with F harmonic minor starting on F.

[Practice check]
The exercise and tempo target are curriculum practice tasks, not transcriptions or claims about the artist's own routine. BPM means quarter notes. Start slower, then use the stated task for self-assessment; listen for missing notes, unintended strings, pitch errors and loss of pulse.

[Sources]
Marty Friedman, Exploring the Phrygian-Dominant Mode: https://www.guitarworld.com/magazine/betcha-cant-play-marty-friedman-explores-phrygian-dominant-mode
Marty Friedman, Finding Your Path to Musical Individuality: https://www.guitarworld.com/magazine/full-shred-marty-friedman-finding-your-path
steps.successCriteria: Record four phrases at 60 BPM; identify Db as flat 2, E as major 3 and the shared notes with F harmonic minor, with intentional resolutions. Use two consecutive clean takes unless another count is specified.

steps.title: Diminished scale fluency
steps.description:
[What it is]
A diminished scale has eight notes alternating whole and half steps.

[Why it matters]
Use one specified form first and distinguish it from a four-note diminished arpeggio. This is an additional colour, not a claim that it defines all Friedman solos.

[How to practice]
Learn A whole-half diminished: A-B-C-D-Eb-F-Gb-Ab. Over an Adim7 drone play the notes as eighths, then select A-C-Eb-Gb alone. In a second comparison start the same collection on Ab to hear the half-whole ordering.

[Practice check]
The exercise and tempo target are curriculum practice tasks, not transcriptions or claims about the artist's own routine. BPM means quarter notes. Start slower, then use the stated task for self-assessment; listen for missing notes, unintended strings, pitch errors and loss of pulse.

[Sources]
Guitar World, 6 Scales from Around the World (educator-authored studies, not Friedman transcriptions): https://www.guitarworld.com/lessons/6-scales-from-around-the-world-that-every-guitar-player-should-know
steps.successCriteria: Record each ordering and the arpeggio twice at 60 BPM; state the eight scale notes and four chord tones, and explain which interval comes first. Use two consecutive clean takes unless another count is specified.

steps.title: Japanese pentatonic variants
steps.description:
[What it is]
This step studies the common guitar-teaching Hirajoshi collection and a rotation of its five pitches.

[Why it matters]
These intervals provide a specific alternative to minor pentatonic. They are not a complete account of Japanese music and do not make a phrase automatically sound like Friedman.

[How to practice]
Over A compare A minor pentatonic A-C-D-E-G with A Hirajoshi A-B-C-E-F. Write two bars emphasizing B-C and E-F. Then use the same Hirajoshi pitches over F: F-A-B-C-E, listening to the changed function. The linked skipping exercise only supports navigation.

[Practice check]
The exercise and tempo target are curriculum practice tasks, not transcriptions or claims about the artist's own routine. BPM means quarter notes. Start slower, then use the stated task for self-assessment; listen for missing notes, unintended strings, pitch errors and loss of pulse.

[Sources]
Guitar World, 6 Scales from Around the World (educator-authored studies, not Friedman transcriptions): https://www.guitarworld.com/lessons/6-scales-from-around-the-world-that-every-guitar-player-should-know
steps.successCriteria: Record four bars over A and four over F at 60 BPM; list both five-note sets, locate the semitone pairs and explain the changed tonal centre. Use two consecutive clean takes unless another count is specified.

steps.title: Chromatic approach notes
steps.description:
[What it is]
A chromatic approach uses a single neighbouring semitone to reach a target.

[Why it matters]
Friedman demonstrates reaching chord tones from below with bends. Here you choose the destination before adding the ornament.

[How to practice]
Over Am compare D#-E and G#-A, first as fretted eighth-note pairs and then as semitone bends. Put the target on beat 2 after an approach on the and of 1; hold, then rest beat 4.

[Practice check]
The exercise and tempo target are curriculum practice tasks, not transcriptions or claims about the artist's own routine. BPM means quarter notes. Start slower, then use the stated task for self-assessment; listen for missing notes, unintended strings, pitch errors and loss of pulse.

[How to practice]

A sequence repeats a chosen order of scale notes and can then vary that order.

[Why it matters]

[How to practice]
Using A-B-C-E-F, play A-C-B-E then B-E-C-F as eighth-note cells. Repeat them, change the final cell to end on A and insert a full beat of rest; write the complete four-bar rhythm.

steps.title: Sweep arpeggio clarity
steps.description:
[What it is]
Sweeping carries a picking stroke through adjacent strings while releasing each previous note.

[Why it matters]
Retain this as a controlled tool, not a defining Friedman requirement. His lessons both demonstrate a brief sweep and criticise predictable repeated up-and-down arpeggios.

[How to practice]
Sweep G14-B13-e12 as an A minor triad in eighth-note triplets, then stop. Compare with separate strokes, and append a held melody note after each version rather than looping the arpeggio indefinitely.

[How to practice]

steps.title: Alternate-economy transitions

This step compares strict alternating strokes with same-direction crossings.

[Why it matters]
The choice should serve a phrase. Technique labels do not require you to reproduce a particular posture or use economy picking everywhere.

[How to practice]
Play G5-G7-G9-B5-B7-B8 ascending as eighth-note triplets. Compare D-U-D-U-D-U with D-U-D-D-U-D. Add a held target after the group and choose the more controllable version for that phrase.

steps.title: Inverted arpeggio shapes
steps.description:
[What it is]
An inverted arpeggio begins on a chord tone other than the root.

[Why it matters]
The changed register and first note give a familiar harmony a different contour without requiring a different chord.

[How to practice]
Over Am play A-C-E, C-E-A and E-A-C as eighth-note triplets followed by a beat of rest. Find comfortable three-string fingerings and end a two-bar phrase on E.

steps.title: Diminished arpeggio sequences
steps.description:
[What it is]
A diminished seventh arpeggio repeats minor thirds between four chord tones.

[Why it matters]
Its symmetry provides a compact tension gesture, but the resolution must be planned rather than left to the fingering pattern.

[How to practice]
Use B-D-F-Ab over E7, then move Ab to A as Am arrives. Play one bar of eighth-note arpeggio tones and one bar resolving to A-C-E. Compare with the eight-note scale from the earlier step.

[What it is]
Legato linking joins chord-tone fragments with slurs or slides while deliberately articulating string changes.

steps.title: Arpeggio phrasing dynamics
steps.description:
[What it is]
Dynamics and rests turn chord-tone movement into a phrase with emphasis.

[Why it matters]
An arpeggio need not be a continuous burst. Connect its intensity to the note that matters in the harmony.

[How to practice]
Over Am-F, one bar each, play four eighth-note chord tones quietly and hold one target for two beats with a stronger attack. Use C as a shared target first, then choose a different chord tone for each chord.

steps.title: Motivic development
steps.description:
[What it is]
Motivic development changes a recognisable short idea across a longer phrase.

[Why it matters]
Friedman advocates modifying familiar material to make it personal. Specify what changes so variation is intentional.

[How to practice]
Write two bars with three or four notes. Make three versions changing respectively the rhythm, final pitch and articulation; repeat the original at the end to create ten bars.

steps.title: Silence and space
steps.description:
[What it is]
Space is a written or deliberately placed rest between musical ideas.

[Why it matters]
A pause makes the next entrance and sustained note meaningful; do not fill every gap with a scale run.

[How to practice]
Over Am-F-C-G, one bar each, allow at most two note attacks per bar and at least one full beat of silence. Sustain or bend a note as desired, but fully stop it during the written rest.

[Practice check]

steps.title: Dynamic microphrasing
steps.description:
[What it is]
Microphrasing adjusts the relative emphasis and duration of notes within a short melody.

[Why it matters]
A small change can alter the direction of a phrase without introducing another technique or more notes.

[How to practice]
Write a two-bar A-C-E melody with a held E. Record it with A emphasized, then with E emphasized, keeping the basic rhythm. Make a third version shortening the approach notes and leaving the held E unchanged.

[Practice check]

steps.title: Vibrato placement choices
steps.description:
[What it is]
Vibrato placement decides which note receives vibrato and when it begins.

[Why it matters]
This applies the earlier pitch-control step to a musical choice. Not every sustained note needs the same treatment.

[How to practice]
Play the same two-bar melody three ways: no vibrato, vibrato immediately on the final note, and vibrato delayed by two beats. Keep its speed and width consistent when it begins.

[Practice check]

steps.title: Tone shaping for sustain
steps.description:
[What it is]
Sustain is the audible continuation of a note after its attack.

[Why it matters]
Keep the fundamental clear while preserving bends and pauses. Equipment can assist; equal sustain with and without gain is not a reasonable universal requirement.

[How to practice]
Hold one note for four beats at 60 BPM and stop it on the next downbeat. Compare two moderate gain settings and two pickup/volume choices one at a time, then place the selected sound over a backing track. The linked vibrato exercise supports touch, not amp setup.

[Practice check]

Delay repeats a played sound after a chosen interval.

[How to practice]

steps.title: Friedmanesque improvisation
steps.description:
[What it is]
Improvisation combines chosen melodic targets with varied approaches and articulation in real time.

[Why it matters]
The result should be judged by audible decisions, not whether someone guesses the artist name. Use the preceding studies as material for your own response.

[How to practice]
Over Am-F-C-G at 70 BPM, improvise 16 bars with a recurring short motif, at least two semitone approaches to chord tones, one register change and one full-beat rest every four bars. Listen back and select one idea to develop in a second take.

steps.title: Arrangement for band context
steps.description:
[What it is]
An arrangement assigns a role to the guitar within a complete accompaniment.

[Why it matters]
A lead has to leave room for other parts and enter at the right point. Chord-tone exercises alone do not establish a usable band arrangement.

[How to practice]
Build a 16-bar sketch at 70 BPM: four bars supporting the backing, eight bars of lead and four returning to support. Write chords, entry cues and effect changes; use a band or a backing track and compare guitar-alone with the full mix.

[Practice check]

steps.title: Live phrasing reproduction
steps.description:
[What it is]
Live reproduction repeats selected articulation and timing choices in a performance context.

[Why it matters]
This tests whether an excerpt is reliable beyond isolated practice. A separate recovery trial checks musical navigation rather than perfect copying alone.

[How to practice]
Use one repertoire excerpt at its established practice speed. Rehearse in your normal performance position with the same backing and effect changes. In a separate take, deliberately leave out a phrase and rejoin at a marked entry.

[Practice check]
The exercise and tempo target are curriculum practice tasks, not transcriptions or claims about the artist's own routine. BPM means quarter notes. Start slower, then use the stated task for self-assessment; listen for missing notes, unintended strings, pitch errors and loss of pulse.

steps.title: Original composition in style
steps.description:
[What it is]
An original composition develops a melody through a complete, playable form.

[Why it matters]
This is the final transfer from technique and repertoire to authorship. It should reveal your choices rather than concatenate copied solo fragments.

[How to practice]
Write 32 bars in 4/4 at 70 BPM: 8-bar theme, 8-bar development, 8-bar contrasting lead and 8-bar return. Include a semitone approach bend, delayed vibrato, an interval leap, a chord-tone arpeggio fragment and planned rests. Write the chord chart and distinguish original material from any quoted reference.

[Practice check]
The exercise and tempo target are curriculum practice tasks, not transcriptions or claims about the artist's own routine. BPM means quarter notes. Start slower, then use the stated task for self-assessment; listen for missing notes, unintended strings, pitch errors and loss of pulse.

[What you can do now]
Shape melody with controlled approaches, releases and vibrato; choose interval and arpeggio colours over stated harmony; reproduce three bounded repertoire excerpts at documented learning speeds; and write and perform a complete original short form. Full album-speed solos remain a further goal, not the promise of this roadmap.
